title: Story
text:
Analysis: The Two-Way Technological Surge
Tracing Major League Baseball from 2005 (bottom left) to 2025 (top right) reveals an unmistakable diagonal migration: the game simultaneously produced significantly higher strikeout rates and higher exit velocities. Rather than giving an edge to only pitchers or only hitters, tracking technology elevated both disciplines at once. Pitchers leveraged spin tracking and release metrics to drive league average strikeouts from 6.55 K/9 in 2005 to 8.61 K/9 in 2025 (a 31.5% increase). Concurrently, hitters used launch angle and exit velocity analytics to optimize swing paths for hard contact, lifting average hard-hit rates from 30.2% up to 42.1%. This trajectory confirms that technology did not simply tilt the scale toward one side—it redefined the physical standards of the sport.

title: About
text:
Data Sources
The data for this project comes from two primary sources: historical player and pitching statistics from the Lahman Baseball Database (accessed via the Lahman R package), and modern batted-ball tracking metrics (such as exit velocity and hard-hit rates) from MLB’s Baseball Savant / Statcast. Together, these datasets allow us to compare pre-Statcast (2005–2014) and Statcast-era (2015–2025) trends across Major League Baseball.

title: Context of the Statistics
text:
Select Season:

Understanding the metrics used throughout this analysis helps clarify how Major League Baseball has evolved. Here is what each statistic measures and why it matters in modern baseball.

title: Context of the Statistics
text:
Strikeouts per 9 Innings (K/9)

What it is: The average number of strikeouts a pitcher records for every 9 innings pitched. \[\text{K/9} = \frac{\text{Strikeouts} \times 9}{\text{Innings Pitched}}\]
Why it matters: Strikeouts are the purest measure of pitching dominance because they take the defense and ballpark dimensions out of the equation. As pitchers gained access to pitch-tracking data, league-wide K/9 rose significantly.

title: Context of the Statistics
text:
Hard-Hit Percentage (Hard-Hit %)

What it is: The proportion of batted balls hit with an exit velocity of 95 mph or greater. \[\text{Hard-Hit \%} = \frac{\text{Batted Balls with Exit Velocity} \ge 95\text{ mph}}{\text{Total Batted Balls}} \times 100\]
Pre-Statcast vs. Statcast measurement:

Pre-Statcast (2005–2014): Tracked by Baseball Info Solutions (BIS) scouts manually classifying contact into soft, medium, or hard trajectories through video analysis.
Statcast Era (2015–Present): Tracked automatically using radar and high-speed cameras to record exact exit velocities.

Why it matters: Exit velocity is the strongest predictor of offensive success. Balls struck at 95+ mph produce the vast majority of extra-base hits and home runs.

title: Context of the Statistics
text:
Whiff Rate

What it is: The percentage of total swings where a batter swings and misses completely. \[\text{Whiff Rate} = \frac{\text{Swings and Misses}}{\text{Total Swings}} \times 100\]
Why it matters: Unlike batting average or overall contact, whiff rate pinpoints a batter’s vulnerability against specific pitch types and zone locations—such as high fastballs or low breaking balls outside the zone.

title: Context of the Statistics
text:
The Statcast Context
Prior to 2015, player evaluation relied on box-score results and scout observation. The introduction of Statcast in all 30 MLB stadiums equipped teams with automated optical cameras and radar to track:

Pitch movement & spin rate: Helping pitchers design sharper, higher-rising fastballs that create more swings and misses.
Batted-ball trajectories (exit velocity & launch angle): Helping hitters optimize their swing paths to elevate balls with high exit velocities.

This data revolution explains why the league migrated diagonally toward higher strikeouts and harder-hit balls at the same time.

title: Players
text:
Player Strike Zone Case Studies
How did elite hitters respond to the Statcast era? By examining pitch-by-pitch tracking data across pre- and post-Statcast seasons, we trace how superstars like Mike Trout, Paul Goldschmidt, and J.D. Martinez adapted their swing decisions and zone coverage.


Mike Trout (2014 vs. 2019 MVP)Paul Goldschmidt (Pre- vs. Post-Statcast MVP)J.D. Martinez (Pre- vs. Post-Statcast Breakout)


Analyzing Mike Trout’s strike zone between 2014 and 2019 reveals how pitch-tracking data refined modern plate discipline and run production. Hitters learned to become hyper-selective—focusing swings on pitches in the heart of the zone where they do maximum damage, while laying off pitcher-friendly edge locations. Comparing his swing decisions directly with his batting average highlights where his selectivity paid off.


















Between 2014 and 2019, Trout dialed his aggression into the middle of the plate—increasing his swing rate in the heart of the zone from 62.7% to 77.4%—while being far more patient on elevated inside pitches (dropping from 54.5% to 36.8%). This selectivity mirrored his results: in 2014, Trout was lethal in the lower and middle regions of the zone (hitting .456 low-middle, .440 low-inside, and .431 in the heart), but struggled on elevated pitches, batting just .053 up-middle. By 2019, Trout dramatically improved his coverage of high pitches—raising his up-middle batting average to .257—while hitting .435 on pitches low-away.


Paul Goldschmidt provides a compelling look at how an elite slugger adapted his swing decisions across nearly a decade of pitch tracking. In his 2013 breakout season with the Arizona Diamondbacks (where he was the NL MVP runner-up), Goldschmidt was particularly eager to attack pitches elevated in the zone, recording a 76.7% swing rate in the upper-middle quadrant and 71.1% mid-in. By his 2022 NL MVP campaign with the St. Louis Cardinals, Goldschmidt adopted a more balanced approach—maintaining a 66.8% swing rate in the heart of the zone while becoming more selective on low and away pitches (49.5% swing rate).


















Comparing his 2013 and 2022 seasons reveals how Goldschmidt developed a patient, disciplined approach across the strike zone—remaining aggressive in the heart (66.8%) while cutting swings on outer-edge chase zones. Examining his batting average highlights his shift from a high-ball hitter in Arizona to an all-fields, lower-zone punisher in St. Louis. In 2013, Goldschmidt crushed pitches in the upper third of the strike zone, hitting .432 up-and-away and .405 up-middle. In 2022, pitchers combated his high-ball power, forcing Goldschmidt to adjust down—where he batted .397 in the heart, .391 low-middle, and .350 low-and-away.


After overhauling his swing mechanics prior to the 2014 season, J.D. Martinez emerged as one of baseball’s premier sluggers. By his 2018 championship season with the Boston Red Sox, Statcast data and launch angle optimization helped him refine his plate aggression even further.


















Comparing Martinez’s 2014 breakout in Detroit with his 2018 championship season in Boston highlights how his refined plate discipline fueled elite production. Martinez became markedly more aggressive on pitches elevated in the zone—increasing his swing rate up-and-in from 73.9% to 82.6%—while demonstrating greater patience low-and-in (dropping from 78.6% to 68.3%). Most dramatically, Statcast-driven launch angle optimization helped him expand his damage zone to the outer half: his batting average on pitches up-and-away surged from .000 in 2014 to .526 in 2018, alongside a .517 mark middle-inside.

title: Baseball Analysis
text:
The Statcast Era
The introduction of Major League Baseball’s Statcast system in 2015 revolutionized how the sport is measured and played. By deploying high-resolution cameras and radar across every ballpark, Statcast enabled the tracking of granular metrics like exit velocity, launch angle, and pitch spin rates on every play.

This project examines how key baseball statistics evolved alongside this technological shift. By comparing trends across the pre-Statcast era (2005–2014) and post-Statcast era (2015–2025), we analyze whether the availability of tracking data coincided with noticeable changes in pitching strikeout rates (K/9) and hitter hard-hit percentages.



⚡ Pitching Evolution

+19.7% K/9 Increase
League average K/9 jumped from 7.21 to 8.63 as spin and movement tracking proliferated.






💥 Hitting Evolution

+26.2% Hard-Hit Surge
Hard-hit rate rose from 30.5% to 38.5% as launch angle and exit velocity became focal points.





⚡ Pitching: Strikeout Rates (K/9)💥 Hitting: Hard-Hit Rates (%)











Each point represents an individual pitcher-season (minimum 30 IP), displaying real pitcher-level variation across thousands of observations. The dashed line traces the annual league average K/9 across the pre-Statcast and post-Statcast eras. Use the dropdown menu to choose individual teams and see their specific pitchers and franchise average.
Between the pre-Statcast era (2005–2014) and the post-Statcast era (2015–2025), average pitcher strikeout rates increased from 7.21 to 8.63 K/9, representing a 19.7% increase across eras (and a 31.5% increase from 6.55 in 2005 to 8.61 in 2025).












Each point represents a qualifying hitter’s individual hard-hit rate for that season, showing real individual-level variation across 4,251 player-seasons. The dashed line traces the annual league average across the pre-Statcast era (BIS video-scouted Hard%) and the Statcast era (radar-measured exit velocity ≥ 95 mph). Use the dropdown menu to choose individual teams and see their specific hitters and franchise average.
Average hard-hit rates rose from 30.5% in the pre-Statcast era to 38.5% in the Statcast era—a 26.2% relative increase (an 8.0 percentage-point gain, climbing to 42.1% by 2025). Note that part of this shift coincides with the change in data measurement (scout observation vs. automated radar tracking).
